rationale: Defines 'major ICT-related incident', one of the review triggers; it helps to apply the trigger but is not needed to name it.
Sets the duty to have 'a sound, comprehensive and well-documented ICT risk management framework': what is reviewed, but neither the frequency nor the triggers.

The framework 'shall be documented and reviewed at least once a year' and also 'upon the occurrence of major ICT-related incidents, and following supervisory instructions or conclusions derived from relevant digital operational resilience testing or audit processes': the regular cycle and the extra triggers asked for.
Same 'at least yearly' wording, but the object is 'the risk scenarios impacting them', not the ICT risk management framework.
Requires to 'regularly review their ICT business continuity policy and ICT response and recovery plans': another document, tempting only because of 'review'.
Requires 'post ICT-related incident reviews after a major ICT-related incident disrupts their core activities': a review of the incident, not of the framework.
Mandates standards on 'the content and format of the report on the review of the ICT risk management framework': the report, not the calendar.

Lexical twin: the simplified framework is 'reviewed periodically and upon the occurrence of major ICT-related incidents', but it only applies to the entities listed in Article 16(1); a mid-sized bank is not among them, so 'periodically' would be a wrong answer here.
'ICT third-party service provider' means 'an undertaking providing ICT services': the vendor is one, and the mapping is evident.

Defines 'critical or important function', a function whose disruption 'would materially impair' the entity's performance or the continuity of its services: it maps the core banking platform to the condition that triggers the exit and contract rules.
Lead-in that carries the duty: contractual arrangements on ICT services 'may be terminated in any of the following circumstances'; the circumstances are its points.
Termination circumstance: 'significant breach by the ICT third-party service provider of applicable laws, regulations or contractual terms'.

Termination circumstance: circumstances found while monitoring ICT third-party risk that are 'deemed capable of altering the performance of the functions provided', including material changes affecting the provider.
Termination circumstance: the provider's 'evidenced weaknesses pertaining to its overall ICT risk management', in particular on the availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality of data.
Termination circumstance: where 'the competent authority can no longer effectively supervise the financial entity' because of the arrangement.

The bank's own planning: 'For ICT services supporting critical or important functions, financial entities shall put in place exit strategies', covering provider failure, service deterioration and termination under paragraph 7.

The rule lives in this lead-in: financial entities 'shall ensure that they are able to exit contractual arrangements without:' the harms its points name, so by the list rule the lead-in takes the top grade.
Exit must happen without 'disruption to their business activities', the need's 'without disrupting'.

Exit without 'limiting compliance with regulatory requirements': one of the three conditions that the exit rule joins under 'without:', so a complete statement of what the bank must ensure includes it.
Exit must happen without 'detriment to the continuity and quality of services provided to clients', the need's concern for customers.
Exit plans 'shall be comprehensive, documented' and 'sufficiently tested and reviewed periodically': a direct requirement on the bank's own planning.

Requires 'transition plans enabling them to remove the contracted ICT services and the relevant data' and 'transfer them to alternative providers or reincorporate them in-house': the switch or insourcing asked for.
Requires 'appropriate contingency measures in place to maintain business continuity': a direct requirement on what the bank must have in place.
Before contracting, consider whether the provider is 'not easily substitutable': related to switching, but a pre-contract assessment.
Lead-in for the minimum content of every ICT services contract: it 'shall include at least the following elements'.

The contract must provide for 'access, recovery and return in an easily accessible format' of data 'in the event of the termination of the contractual arrangements': a contract term the switch depends on.
The contract must include 'termination rights and related minimum notice periods for the termination of the contractual arrangements'.

Lead-in: contracts for ICT services 'supporting critical or important functions shall include, in addition to the elements referred to in paragraph 2, at least the following'; a core banking platform supports such functions.

'notice periods and reporting obligations of the ICT third-party service provider', including notice of developments that may impair its service: an early warning that feeds the termination circumstances, not an exit term; context.
The contract must include 'exit strategies, in particular the establishment of a mandatory adequate transition period'.

During the transition period the provider 'will continue providing the respective functions, or ICT services, with a view to reducing the risk of disruption': the 'without disrupting' part of the need.
The transition period must allow 'the financial entity to migrate to another ICT third-party service provider or change to in-house solutions'.

The Lead Overseer assesses arrangements 'which ensure an effective exercise of termination rights by the financial entities': oversight of critical providers, not what the bank's contract and planning must contain.

A further termination case: competent authorities 'may require financial entities to terminate' arrangements, but only those with 'critical ICT third-party service providers', which the need does not say the vendor is; context.
Lead-in of the scope: 'this Regulation applies to the following entities'.
The scope lists 'payment institutions, including payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366': the exempt small payment business is covered.

Lexical twin: 'electronic money institutions, including electronic money institutions exempted pursuant to Directive 2009/110/EC' has the same construction but concerns e-money institutions, not payment institutions.
The entities in points (a) to (t) are the 'financial entities' that the obligations address: context.
The exclusions ('This Regulation does not apply to:') to which paragraph 1 is 'without prejudice'; none covers exempted payment institutions, which confirms the answer; context.
'natural or legal persons exempted pursuant to Articles 2 and 3 of Directive 2014/65/EU' are excluded, but that is the investment-services exemption, not the payment-services one.
Chapter II rules are implemented 'in accordance with the principle of proportionality': a general principle, not the specific lighter regime.
'Articles 5 to 15 of this Regulation shall not apply to' payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366: the full ICT risk management set-up does not apply, a lighter one does.
Lead-in of what those entities must still do ('shall:'); without it the answer would wrongly suggest that they have no ICT risk management duties.
The core of the lighter version: 'put in place and maintain a sound and documented ICT risk management framework'.
Simplified duty to 'continuously monitor the security and functioning of all ICT systems': detail of the lighter version.
Simplified duty to minimise ICT risk with 'sound, resilient and updated ICT systems': detail of the lighter version.
Simplified duty to detect anomalies and handle incidents swiftly: detail of the lighter version.
Simplified duty to 'identify key dependencies on ICT third-party service providers': detail of the lighter version.
Simplified duty to ensure continuity through 'business continuity plans and response and recovery measures': detail of the lighter version.
Simplified duty to 'test, on a regular basis' those plans and controls: detail of the lighter version.
Simplified duty to apply test conclusions and run awareness and training: detail of the lighter version.
The simplified framework is 'reviewed periodically and upon the occurrence of major ICT-related incidents': detail of the lighter regime.

The national exemption the founder relies on ('Member States may exempt ... natural or legal persons providing payment services'). Whether a complete answer must cite it to map the founder's 'country's exemption' onto DORA's 'exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366' is a judgment the text does not settle.

The need's 'board members' must be mapped to 'members of the management body' in Article 50(5); for an insurer, whose sectoral act is not listed, the definition reaches them only through 'the equivalent persons who effectively run the entity'.
The Lead Overseer's decision 'imposing a periodic penalty payment to compel the critical ICT third-party service provider to comply': a different addressee and authority.

A periodic penalty payment 'up to 1 % of the average daily worldwide turnover' is a maximum, but it is imposed by the Lead Overseer on critical ICT third-party service providers, not on an insurer by its national supervisor.
Competent authorities 'shall have all supervisory, investigatory and sanctioning powers necessary': the general power, without the list.
Lead-in: 'The powers referred to in paragraph 1 shall include at least the following powers to:'.
Access to documents and data: an investigatory power, not a sanction or corrective measure.
On-site inspections or investigations: an investigatory power, not a sanction or corrective measure.
The supervisor can 'require corrective and remedial measures for breaches of the requirements of this Regulation'.

'Member States shall lay down rules establishing appropriate administrative penalties and remedial measures': who sets the sanctions, and why the maximum fine lives in national law, the gap of this need.
Penalties must be 'effective, proportionate and dissuasive': a standard, not a measure or an amount.
Lead-in: Member States 'shall confer on competent authorities the power to apply at least the following administrative penalties or remedial measures'.
An order 'to cease conduct that is in breach of this Regulation and to desist from a repetition of that conduct'.
'the temporary or permanent cessation of any practice or conduct' contrary to the Regulation.
'adopt any type of measure, including of pecuniary nature', to ensure continued compliance: the only mention of pecuniary measures, with no amount.
Requiring 'existing data traffic records held by a telecommunication operator': an investigative measure, not a sanction the board needs to know.
'issue public notices, including public statements indicating the identity of the natural or legal person and the nature of the breach'.

Penalties and measures can apply, 'subject to the conditions provided for in national law, to members of the management body, and to other individuals who under national law are responsible for the breach': board members can be held responsible.
Decisions must be 'properly reasoned' and 'subject to a right of appeal': procedure, not a measure.
Criteria for 'the type and level' of a penalty (gravity, responsibility, financial strength): how a fine is sized, not its maximum.

Paragraph 3 of Article 50 is 'without prejudice to the right of Member States to impose criminal penalties in accordance with Article 52', and this derogation lets them 'decide not to lay down rules for administrative penalties' for breaches subject to criminal penalties: it can change which sanctions the supervisor imposes.
Final penalty decisions are published on the authority's website: a consequence, dispensable.
Defines custody and administration as 'the safekeeping or controlling, on behalf of clients, of crypto-assets': the need's wording maps to it almost literally.
The 'register of positions' opened for each client, from which the statement is drawn: context.

A 'summary of the custody policy shall be made available to clients at their request in an electronic format': on request and electronic like the statement, but it is the custody policy, not a statement of holdings.

Custodians 'shall provide their clients, at least once every three months and at the request of the client concerned, with a statement of position of the crypto-assets recorded in the name of those clients': the frequency and the on-request statement.
Information 'about operations on crypto-assets that require a response' from clients: other client reporting, dispensable.
'periodic statements' of 'the portfolio management activities carried out on their behalf' belong to portfolio management, not custody.

Near twin: that periodic statement is 'provided every three months, except' where the client can see online valuations; same frequency, different service and an exception that custody statements do not have.
The baseline: 'A person shall not provide crypto-asset services, within the Union, unless' authorised or otherwise allowed; the exemption only makes sense against it.
Authorisation as a crypto-asset service provider under Article 63: the route the firm does not have; context.
A person that is not a crypto-asset service provider shall not 'issue marketing communications' suggesting that it is one: a further limit on its emails, dispensable.
Providers 'shall be allowed to provide crypto-asset services throughout the Union' without physical presence, but only authorised crypto-asset service providers.

Where a client in the Union 'initiates at its own exclusive initiative the provision of a crypto-asset service' by a third-country firm, 'the requirement for authorisation under Article 59 shall not apply' to serving that client.

A firm that 'solicits clients or prospective clients in the Union, regardless of the means of communication used for the solicitation, promotion or advertising' is not serving them at their own initiative: promotional emails put the exemption at risk.
Contract clauses or disclaimers cannot turn solicitation into exclusive initiative: context.

'A client's own exclusive initiative' does 'not entitle a third-country firm to market new types of crypto-assets or crypto-asset services to that client': the emails about new tokens and services are not allowed.
ESMA guidelines will specify 'the situations in which a third-country firm is deemed to solicit clients': useful, but outside the articles.
The notification for providing services 'in more than one Member State' applies to an authorised crypto-asset service provider, not to a third-country firm.
Defines transfer services as transferring crypto-assets 'from one distributed ledger address or account to another': it maps the activity but gives no data requirements.
Requires procedures 'to comply with the provisions of national law transposing Directive (EU) 2015/849': anti-money-laundering duties live outside these articles; no transfer data.
Transfer service providers 'shall conclude an agreement with their clients' on modalities, security and fees; nothing on the data that must accompany a transfer or on self-hosted addresses.
ESMA guidelines on transfer 'procedures and policies, including the rights of clients': not the data that travel with a transfer, and outside the articles.
'the information or unique identifier to be provided by the payment service user' for a PSD2 payment order, not sender and recipient data for crypto-asset transfers.
'information relating to the payee' is what a payer receives about a PSD2 payment transaction, not data that must travel with a crypto-asset transfer.

DORA applies to 'crypto-asset service providers as authorised under' MiCA, which makes the yearly testing of Article 11(6)(a) bind the exchange directly. Whether the answer needs it, or MiCA's 'set up pursuant to Articles 11 and 12' already imports the testing duty, is a reading the text does not settle.
The 'comprehensive ICT business continuity policy' forming part of the overall business continuity policy: context for the policy.
Aims of the ICT business continuity policy under DORA; the need asks for the aims under the crypto rules.
'implement associated ICT response and recovery plans': the second of the plans the crypto rules point to.
'put in place, maintain and periodically test appropriate ICT business continuity plans': the first of the plans the crypto rules point to.
Lead-in of the testing duties: 'As part of their comprehensive ICT risk management, financial entities shall:'.

'test the ICT business continuity plans and the ICT response and recovery plans' 'at least yearly, as well as in the event of any substantive changes to ICT systems supporting critical or important functions': how often the plans are tested.
Testing plans must include 'scenarios of cyber-attacks and switchovers': what is tested, not how often.
'regularly review' the policy and plans in light of test results: review, not testing frequency.

Lead-in by which financial entities 'shall develop and document' backup and recovery procedures, for 'ensuring the restoration of ICT systems and data with minimum downtime': part of the Article 12 that the crypto rules cite; context.
'Testing of the backup procedures and restoration and recovery procedures and methods shall be undertaken periodically': testing of backups, not the yearly testing of the plans.
'test, on a regular basis' belongs to the simplified framework of Article 16(1), whose list of entities does not include crypto-asset service providers.
Lexical twin: the same continuity wording, but addressed to 'Issuers of asset-referenced tokens', not crypto-asset service providers.
The general duty to 'ensure continuity and regularity' with 'resilient and secure ICT systems'; the aims of the policy itself are stated in the second subparagraph, so this is context.

Providers 'shall establish a business continuity policy, which shall include ICT business continuity plans as well as ICT response and recovery plans set up pursuant to Articles 11 and 12 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2554', aiming at 'the preservation of essential data and functions and the maintenance of crypto-asset services' or their timely recovery.
The trading systems of a trading platform must be 'subject to effective business continuity arrangements': it applies only if the exchange operates a trading platform; dispensable.
'Within 10 business days of receiving a request for a refund' is the deadline for refund requests on payee-initiated transactions, not for complaint replies.
Complaints 'to the competent authorities' about infringements: a different channel, with no reply deadline for the provider.
Providers must apply 'adequate and effective complaint resolution procedures': context, no deadline.

Reply 'at the latest within 15 business days of receipt of the complaint'; 'In exceptional situations' beyond the control of the provider, a holding reply, and 'the deadline for receiving the final reply shall not exceed 35 business days'.

'Member States may introduce or maintain rules on dispute resolution procedures that are more advantageous to the payment service user': national law can shorten the deadline, so 15 days is a maximum.
Requires informing the user 'about at least one ADR entity': nothing about the reply deadline or its extension.
ADR procedures for disputes: nothing about the provider's reply deadline.
Defines 'direct debit'; the need uses the term in its ordinary sense: context.
Notification 'no later than 13 months after the debit date' applies to unauthorised or incorrectly executed transactions; the gym debit was authorised.
A refund 'no later than by the end of the following business day' is for unauthorised payment transactions, not authorised direct debits.

'a payer is entitled to a refund' of 'an authorised payment transaction which was initiated by or through a payee', 'if both of the following conditions are met': a signed mandate does not rule out a refund.
Condition: 'the authorisation did not specify the exact amount of the payment transaction'.
Condition: the amount 'exceeded the amount the payer could reasonably have expected taking into account the previous spending pattern', as with the much larger gym debit.
The payer bears 'the burden of proving such conditions are met' on request: practical detail.
The refund is 'the full amount' with a value date no later than the debit date: detail.
'for direct debits as referred to in Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 260/2012, the payer has an unconditional right to a refund within the time limits laid down in Article 77'.
Exception: a framework contract may provide that 'the payer has no right to a refund' where the conditions in its points are met; it can change the answer.
Exception condition: consent given 'directly to the payment service provider'.
Exception condition: information on the future transaction provided 'for at least 4 weeks before the due date'.
Direct debits in other currencies may carry more favourable refund rights: context.
The payer 'can request the refund' 'for a period of 8 weeks from the date on which the funds were debited': six weeks is within the limit.
'Within 10 business days of receiving a request for a refund, the payment service provider shall either refund the full amount' or justify the refusal.
The right to refuse 'shall not apply' to the unconditional direct-debit refund of the fourth subparagraph of Article 76(1).
The 15-business-day deadline is for replying to complaints, not for answering a refund request.
